intro: か marks something open, not yet settled. At the end of a sentence it turns a statement into a question; between nouns it offers alternatives, only one of which is meant; after a question word it turns "what" into "something"; inside a sentence it wraps a question you do not know the answer to. Wherever か appears, an answer is still missing.

skills.rule: Add か to the end of a polite sentence to make it a question; the word order does not change.
skills.explain:
Take any polite sentence and add か: 学生です becomes 学生ですか, 行きます becomes 行きますか. The same か closes questions with a question word: 何を食べますか. No inversion, no extra word, and in writing a plain 。 after か is normal.

In casual speech, か after a plain verb or adjective sounds blunt or rough (行くか？), so friends drop it and use rising intonation (行く？) or の (行くの？). After a plain noun or na-adjective, だ never comes before a question か: 暇か？ (blunt) or 暇？, never 暇だか.

The boundary is with ね and よ. か asks for information you do not have; ね checks something you think the listener shares; よ tells the listener something they do not know. 行きますか "Are you going?", 行きますね "You're going, right?", 行きますよ "I'm going, you know." A negative question with ませんか is an invitation: 一緒に行きませんか "Would you like to come with me?"
patterns: [question word] ... ですか / ますか

examples.jp: 学生[がくせい]です{か}。
examples.en: Are you a student?

examples.jp: これは何[なん]です{か}。
examples.en: What is this?

examples.jp: 駅[えき]はどこです{か}。
examples.en: Where is the station?

examples.jp: 明日[あした]も来[き]ます{か}。
examples.en: Are you coming tomorrow too?

examples.jp: 一緒[いっしょ]に昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べません{か}。
examples.en: Would you like to have lunch together?

contrast.note: ね asks the listener to agree with something you already believe (いい天気ですね). It cannot ask for information you lack, so it cannot close a question-word question in place of か (何ですね is wrong).
よ hands the listener new information: 行きますよ "I'm going, you know". It states; か asks.
Casual questions use rising の (どこに行くの？) instead of か. In polite speech the question marker is か.

mistakes.note: A question word needs か. ね only seeks agreement and cannot ask "what".

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]、暇[ひま]だ{か}。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]、暇[ひま]です{か}。
mistakes.note: だ never comes right before a question か. Use です か, or casually just 暇？ with rising intonation.

skills.tip: Do you want an answer you do not have? End with か. Want agreement: ね. Telling them: よ.

skills.rule: AかB means "A or B": a choice where only one of the items is meant.
skills.explain:
か between nouns means "or": コーヒーか紅茶 "coffee or tea". The whole phrase then takes the particle its role needs, after the last item: 月曜日か火曜日に来てください. You may repeat か after the last item (AかBか) to stress that it is one or the other. か can also join whole clauses: 電車で行くかバスで行くか決めてください.

The real boundary is with と and や, which add items together. AとB is both, AやB is several things among others; AかB is one of them. ペンか鉛筆で書いてください lets you use either; ペンと鉛筆 would mean you use both.

When you ask "A or B?" as a question, Japanese usually asks two questions in a row, joined by それとも if you like: コーヒーにしますか、それとも紅茶にしますか. か alone joins the nouns inside one sentence. Rough numbers use it too: 一人か二人 "one or two people".
patterns: A か B か [particle] (one or the other)
[clause] か [clause] か (決める / わかる)

examples.jp: 水[みず]{か}お茶[ちゃ]をください。
examples.en: Water or tea, please.

examples.jp: ペン{か}鉛筆[えんぴつ]で書[か]いてください。
examples.en: Please write in pen or pencil.

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]{か}バスで行[い]きます。
examples.en: I'll go by train or bus.

examples.jp: 月曜日[げつようび]{か}火曜日[かようび]に来[き]てください。
examples.en: Please come on Monday or Tuesday.

examples.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みは海[うみ]{か}山[やま]に行[い]きたいです。
examples.en: For the summer holidays I want to go to the sea or the mountains.

contrast.note: AとB is both: exactly A and B together. AかB is one of the two.
AやB lists examples that all apply (A, B and so on). AかB picks one.
AもBも means both A and B (or neither, with a negative). It includes every item; か leaves the choice open.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]や明後日[あさって]に電話[でんわ]します。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]{か}明後日[あさって]に電話[でんわ]します。
mistakes.note: You will call on one of the two days, not on both: that is か.

mistakes.bad: ペンと鉛筆[えんぴつ]で書[か]いてください。
mistakes.good: ペン{か}鉛筆[えんぴつ]で書[か]いてください。
mistakes.note: If you mean "either one", と is wrong: it tells the reader to use both.

skills.tip: Will you end up with just one of them? か. All of them? と or や.

skills.rule: Question word + か makes a "some-" word: 何か something, 誰か someone, どこか somewhere, いつか some day, どれか one of them.
skills.explain:
Add か to a question word and it stops asking: 何 "what" becomes 何か "something", 誰 "who" becomes 誰か "someone". In a question they mean "anything / anyone": 何か質問はありますか "Are there any questions?"

が and を are often dropped after these words (誰か来ました, 何か飲みたい); keeping them (誰かが来ました) is also correct. Other particles stay and go after か: どこかに行きたい, 誰かと話したい.

The partner is question word + も with a negative verb, meaning "nothing, nobody, nowhere": 何も食べませんでした, 誰もいません, どこにも行きません. English "I didn't eat anything" tempts learners into 何か, but a negative "not any" is 何も. Keep 何か apart from 何が as well: 何か落ちました "something fell", 何が落ちましたか "what fell?" One kana turns a statement into a question.
patterns: 何か / 誰か / どこか / いつか [verb]
どこか に / 誰か と [verb]
question word + も + negative = nothing / nobody

examples.jp: 何[なに]{か}飲[の]みますか。
examples.en: Would you like something to drink?

examples.jp: 誰[だれ]{か}来[き]ました。
examples.en: Someone came.

examples.jp: いつ{か}日本[にほん]に行[い]きたいです。
examples.en: I want to go to Japan someday.

examples.jp: 何[なに]{か}質問[しつもん]はありますか。
examples.en: Are there any questions?

examples.jp: どこ{か}で会[あ]いましたね。
examples.en: We've met somewhere before, haven't we?

examples.jp: この中[なか]からどれ{か}選[えら]んでください。
examples.en: Please choose one of these.

contrast.note: Question word + も with a negative verb is "nothing / nobody / nowhere": 何も知りません. With か the sentence says something exists; with も it says nothing does.
何が and 誰が keep the question: 誰が来ましたか "Who came?" 誰か来ましたか "Did anyone come?"

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]は何[なに]か食[た]べませんでした。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]は何[なに]{も}食[た]べませんでした。
mistakes.note: "I didn't eat anything" is 何も + negative. 何か is for "something" that exists.

mistakes.bad: すみません、誰[だれ]がいますか。
mistakes.good: すみません、誰[だれ]{か}いますか。
mistakes.note: "Is anyone there?" is 誰か. 誰がいますか asks who exactly is there.

skills.tip: "Some-" or "any-" in a positive sentence or question: question word + か. "No-" with a negative verb: question word + も.

skills.rule: Put a plain-form question inside a sentence with か (question-word questions) or かどうか (yes/no questions), then go on with わかる, 知る, 聞く, 教える or 決める.
skills.explain:
To say "I don't know where she went", put the question in plain form before か: どこに行ったかわかりません. A question with a question word takes か; a yes/no question takes かどうか "whether or not": 来るかどうか聞いてください. In speech plain か also works for yes/no (来るか聞いて), but かどうか is never wrong.

The clause is plain even in a polite sentence: 何時に始まるか教えてください, not 始まりますか. After a noun or na-adjective, drop だ: 誰の傘かわかりません, 静かかどうか.

The clause + か acts like a noun. が and を after it are normally dropped, but は and other particles can follow: 行くかどうかはまだ決めていません. The common mistake is と: と reports words someone said, か wraps an open question. 来ると言いました "said he would come"; 来るか聞きました "asked whether he would come".
patterns: [question-word clause, plain] か わかる / 知っている / 教える
[yes/no clause, plain] かどうか 聞く / 決める

examples.jp: 駅[えき]がどこ{か}わかりますか。
examples.en: Do you know where the station is?

examples.jp: 何時[なんじ]に始[はじ]まる{か}教[おし]えてください。
examples.en: Please tell me what time it starts.

examples.jp: これは誰[だれ]の傘[かさ]{か}知[し]っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know whose umbrella this is?

examples.jp: 明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る{か}どうかわかりません。
examples.en: I don't know whether it will rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんが来[く]る{か}どうか聞[き]いてみます。
examples.en: I'll ask whether Mr Tanaka is coming.

examples.jp: 何[なに]を買[か]う{か}もう決[き]めましたか。
examples.en: Have you decided what to buy yet?

contrast.note: と quotes words or thoughts: 来ると言いました "said he would come". か wraps a question whose answer is open: 来るか聞きました "asked whether he would come".
の turns a known fact into a noun (彼が来たのを知っています "I know that he came"). か turns an unknown into a noun (彼が来たか知りません "I don't know whether he came").

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]がどこですかわかりません。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]がどこ{か}わかりません。
mistakes.note: An embedded question is plain: drop です (and だ) before か.

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さんが来[く]ると聞[き]きました。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さんが来[く]る{か}聞[き]きました。
mistakes.note: With と the sentence means "I heard he is coming". To say "I asked whether he is coming", use か.

skills.tip: Does the English have "whether" or a wh-word in the middle of the sentence? か (yes/no: かどうか). Does it have "that"? と or の.
